**TutorConnect** is a desktop application designed for **freelance private tutors** to organise student contacts, track lesson schedules, and manage parent communications. Optimized for fast typists, it combines the speed of a Command Line Interface (CLI) with the convenience of a Graphical User Interface (GUI).
* **Target User:** Freelance private tutors managing multiple students and parents across different academic levels.
* **Fast Keyboard-Driven Workflow:** Add records, update lesson notes, and query schedules without touching a mouse.
* **Organised Directories:** Group students by subject, grade level, and recurring time slots.
* For the detailed documentation of this project, see the **[TutorConnect Product Website](https://ay2627s1-cs2103t-f08-3.github.io/tp/)**.
* If you are interested in using TutorConnect, see the **[User Guide](docs/UserGuide.md)**.
* If you are interested in contributing or extending this project, see the **[Developer Guide](docs/DeveloperGuide.md)**.

Use this checklist for the affected parts of each PR and for reported bugs. It turns the team's supplied
functionality/feature-flaw guidance into review and verification steps; it is not a guarantee of a bug-free
product or a substitute for the course's current scope rules. Record unverified checks honestly.
1. Reproduce with synthetic data, recording the commit, Java/OS, window size if relevant, exact input,
expected versus actual behavior, and the affected task. Do not attach real student contact data.
2. Decide what should change. Broken implementation is `type.FunctionalityBug`; a missing or inconvenient
design is `type.FeatureFlaw`; an incorrect guide is `type.DocumentationBug` if behavior is appropriate.
A guide change alone does not cure an unusable design. Related symptoms may share one root cause.
3. Propose severity from frequency, affected users, task obstruction, recoverability, and data loss.
Minor clipping can be `severity.VeryLow`; obscuring information needed to distinguish students can
warrant `Low` or higher. Do not classify a crash/data-loss risk as cosmetic merely because input is unusual.
4. Claim `NotInScope` only with the applicable course rule and a user-impact rationale. Do not use it for
a flaw essential to reasonable usefulness, or an unnecessarily worse design with a low-effort improvement.
Low severity is not the same as out of scope. Disputed cases need team/course review.
5. Assign the affected feature owner, agree shared-interface changes, add a reproducing regression test,
then fix and verify. Record remaining product decisions separately from completed repairs.
| Area | Prevention and evidence required when affected |

| Accidental malformed input | Try a missing space between prefixes, copy/paste line breaks, blank values, repeated/unknown prefixes, and concatenated values. Assert a controlled error, no partial profile, unchanged bytes/model/filter/selection, and a usable next command. |

| Extreme input / overflow | Deliberate sabotage alone need not be a course bug; assess whether ordinary mistakes can reach the same path. Exercise values beyond the machine integer range and reject/resolve them before narrowing. Do not spend unbounded effort on artificial resource exhaustion. |

| Long values | Test at the supported maximum and one beyond it, including Unicode code points and long unbroken words. Inspect the real window at minimum size and a normal size. Important values must remain accessible through wrapping, scrolling, or an equivalent usable detail view. |

| Limits and symbols | Justify restrictions against actual users, not parser convenience alone. Try realistic apostrophes, hyphens, combining marks, unit numbers, embedded slashes, and legal-name conventions such as `s/o`. A documented restriction can still be a design flaw. |

| Duplicate detection | Normalize case/Unicode/spaces and canonical phones consistently. Cover duplicate students hidden by a filter. Explain which matches block, warn, or pass; never imply fuzzy identity detection when it is not implemented. |

| Overzealous validation | Prefer warning/acceptance when safe and within the agreed product contract. Review legitimate exceptions before blocking; validate harmful values. Do not silently introduce multiple phones, international support, or other excluded features. |

| Error specificity | Identify the offending parameter and corrective action where practical. Keep missing, blank, repeated, format, invalid value, missing index, duplicate, and save errors distinct and test precedence. Do not relabel a value error as a format error. Propose shared-message changes for owner agreement. |

| Command usability | Assess typing burden and discoverability; consider aliases when useful. Preserve existing case-sensitive command/prefix contracts until an agreed change updates parsers, tests, and UG together. |

| Case and search | Preserve display case but compare names/search keywords case-insensitively. Exercise supported Unicode/space normalization. Confirm documented full-word versus substring behavior and OR versus AND matching; assess usefulness, not only implementation consistency. |

| UG/behavior mismatch | Execute documented examples and compare every relevant limit, message, save/reload promise, and field format with the current branch. Fix either behavior or docs based on intended user value, not whichever change is easiest. |

| Terminal output | Inspect logs during startup, valid input, ordinary errors, and load/save failures. Routine input must not look like an application crash. Avoid echoing raw control characters or contact data; distinguish diagnostic output from the single GUI status. Terminal-only issues can be lower severity, not automatically out of scope. |

| Human-edited data | Verify correct edits load, old records with missing optional fields load, and UUID/order/unrelated fields survive a save/reload. Check malformed syntax, null root/records/tags, duplicate IDs, and invalid known fields. Fail loading cleanly rather than publishing part of the file. |

| Storage safety | Exercise injected write and atomic-replace failures. Check file bytes, in-memory objects, filter, and selection. No-change/read-only commands must not write; do not add a truncate-in-place fallback. |
The baseline for manual editing is the [AB3 User Guide](https://se-education.org/addressbook-level3/UserGuide.html#editing-the-data-file):
valid edits work; invalid edits may lose data as documented. TutorConnect must not promise recovery/backup
features it does not provide. The [human-editable-file constraint](https://nus-cs2103-ay2627-s1.github.io/website/admin/tp-constraints.html#constraint-human-editable-file)

## TutorConnect decisions that remain open to review
The following are current requirements, not exemptions from feature-flaw triage:
- Phones are restricted to one Singapore number per field. The team should confirm the intended users'
contact needs; do not claim all freelance tutors have only Singapore contacts. International or multiple
numbers require an explicit product decision and compatible validation/storage changes.
- Names do not accept `/` or digits, so some legal-name conventions are unsupported. The field must not
be represented as guaranteed legal-name support. Review impact with the team rather than recommending
falsified names or silently expanding a shared grammar.
- Whitespace-delimited letter-plus-slash tokens are reserved prefixes. Embedded slashes such as `12/3`
or `Math/Science` are data, but a value containing a standalone prefix-like token has a limitation.
- Commands/prefixes are lowercase and case-sensitive. Search is case-insensitive, OR-based, and full-word,
not fuzzy. Canonical-equivalence/Unicode search behavior needs explicit verification when changed.
- Duplicate blocking uses normalized name **and** phone. Different names sharing a phone warn but are
accepted; the same name with a different phone is accepted without a fuzzy-name warning. Spelling
variants, nicknames, and real-world identity are not resolved automatically.
Changing these decisions requires owner agreement, examples, tests, and corresponding UG changes.
Documenting a limitation helps set expectations but does not make every limitation acceptable.
- `DataFileSafetyTest` reproduces malformed JSON load paths and checks controlled storage/list errors,
no partial publication, unchanged selection/filter/objects/file bytes, and valid manual-edit round trips.
- `JsonAdaptedTagTest` verifies a null tag name yields validation failure rather than a null-pointer crash.
- `AddStudentEndToEndTest` covers missed prefix separators, accidentally concatenated phones, and values
just beyond name/address limits while checking unchanged state and bytes. Existing tests cover error
precedence, normalized duplicates, shared-phone warnings, and save failures.
- Existing `StudentFieldIntegrationTest`, field-owner tests, and JavaFX acceptance tests cover large
displayed indices, cross-feature preservation, no-change, atomic rollback, and selection/details.
These tests do not certify every visual layout, legal-name use case, locale, or console message. Record
manual evidence or follow-up decisions for those areas before declaring them verified.
For relevant risks, record: scenario; classification and impact; owner/decision; automated test or manual
evidence; result; remaining limitations. Use **passed**, **failed**, **not run**, or **not applicable with reason**.

This project uses Gradle for **build automation and dependency management**. **We recommend reading [this Gradle tutorial from se-edu/guides](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/gradle.html).**
The following commands perform common Gradle tasks.
* **`build`** (also the default task): Compiles, tests, checks style, and builds distributions including
`build/libs/tutorconnect.jar`. It checks the executable manifest and required UI resources using
`verifyShadowJar`. Builds are incremental; `clean` is optional, not an automatic prerequisite.
The Java toolchain targets an installed JDK 25 and Java source encoding is UTF-8 on every platform.
* **`clean`**: Deletes the files created during the previous build tasks (e.g. files in the `build` folder).
* **`shadowJar`**: Uses the Shadow plugin to create the fat JAR file `build/libs/tutorconnect.jar`.
**`runShadow`**: Builds the application as a fat JAR, then runs it.
* **`checkstyleMain`**: Runs the code style check for the main code base.
**`checkstyleTest`**: Runs the code style check for the test code base.
* `./gradlew test`: Runs tests; desktop groups require the F01/F06/F08 environment flags in [Testing](Testing.md).
* `./gradlew clean test`: Cleans the project before running all tests
This project uses GitHub Actions for CI. The necessary workflow configuration files are in `.github/workflows`. No further setup is required.
CI runs `build coverage` on Linux, macOS and Windows. Linux enables all three desktop groups under Xvfb;
the other jobs do not opt into desktop tests. Each successful build uploads `tutorconnect.jar` as a
platform-named workflow artifact. These are review/test artifacts, not automatically published releases.
As part of CI, Gradle generates JaCoCo coverage reports from the tests, and CI uploads the coverage data to Codecov. Codecov then provides information about test coverage.

However, because Codecov is known to run into intermittent problems (e.g., report upload fails) due to issues on the Codecov service side, the CI is configured to pass even if the Codecov task failed. Therefore, developers are advised to check the code coverage levels periodically and take corrective actions if the coverage level falls below desired levels.
To enable Codecov for forks of this project, follow the steps given in [this se-edu guide](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/codecov.html).

* Checks are implemented as executable `check-*` scripts within the `.github` directory. The `run-checks.sh` script will automatically pick up and run files named as such. That is, you can add more such files if you need and the CI will do the rest.
* Check scripts should print out errors in the format `SEVERITY:FILENAME:LINE: MESSAGE`

The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`TutorConnectLauncher`** (consisting of classes [`TutorConnectLauncher`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-F08-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/tutorconnect/TutorConnectLauncher.java) and [`TutorConnectApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-F08-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/tutorconnect/TutorConnectApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.
**How the architecture components interact with each other**
The *Sequence Diagram* below shows how the components interact with each other for the scenario where the user issues the command `delete 1`.
Each of the four main components (also shown in the diagram above),
* defines its *API* in an `interface` with the same name as the Component.
* provides its functionality through a concrete `{Component Name}Manager` class that implements the corresponding API interface.

For example, the `Logic` component defines its API in `Logic.java` and implements it in `LogicManager.java`. Other components interact with a component through its interface rather than its concrete class, preventing them from coupling to that component's implementation, as illustrated in the following partial class diagram.
The sections below give more details of each component.
The **API** of this component is specified in [`Ui.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-F08-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/tutorconnect/ui/Ui.java)
<puml src="diagrams/UiClassDiagram.puml" alt="Structure of the UI Component"/>

The UI consists of a `MainWindow` and its parts: `CommandBox`, `ResultDisplay`, `StudentListPanel` (with one `StudentCard` per row), `StudentDetailsPanel`, `WeeklySchedulePanel` and `StatusBarFooter`. `MainWindow` and the FXML-backed parts inherit from the abstract `UiPart` class, which captures common behavior among classes that represent visible GUI parts. `StudentDetailsPanel` and `WeeklySchedulePanel` are code-built JavaFX `VBox` subclasses without FXML, so they do not extend `UiPart`.

`MainWindow` wires three views of the same register. `StudentListPanel` shows `Logic#getFilteredStudentList()`, which `find`/`filter` narrow and whose order defines visible indices. `StudentDetailsPanel` shows the student whose UUID is `Logic#getSelectedStudentId()`. `WeeklySchedulePanel` shows `Logic#getWeeklySchedule()`, the separately sorted list of every scheduled student. After each command, `MainWindow` passes any `TimetableView` carried by the `CommandResult` to `WeeklySchedulePanel#showDay`, then refreshes selection and details.

The `UI` component uses the JavaFX UI framework. The layouts of these UI parts are defined in matching `.fxml` files in `src/main/resources/view`. For example, [`MainWindow.fxml`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-F08-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/resources/view/MainWindow.fxml) specifies the layout of [`MainWindow`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-F08-3/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/tutorconnect/ui/MainWindow.java).
* executes user commands using the `Logic` component.
* listens for changes to `Model` data so that the UI can be updated with the modified data.
* keeps a reference to the `Logic` component, because the `UI` relies on the `Logic` to execute commands.
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component because it displays `Student` objects from the model.
* keeps the timetable day as UI-only state: `timetable` never reaches the model, storage or the displayed-list predicate.

* `TutorConnectParser` dispatches `add`, `guardian`, `delete` and `edit` to the corresponding concrete
`Parser<T>`. Each returns its matching command; parsing does not save or mutate the model.
* `AddCommandParser` and `GuardianCommandParser` use `StudentParameters` to validate parameter structure
while retaining raw values. `ParserUtil` creates validated contact values and arbitrary-size `Index` objects.
* `DeleteCommandParser` normalizes its single positional argument through `StudentText`, checks missing
or multiple indices, then uses `ParserUtil.parseIndex`. Index syntax and row existence are separate checks:
command execution resolves the index against the currently displayed list using `VisibleIndexResolver`.
* `EditCommandParser` checks raw controls before trimming, recognizes Unicode spaces, and rejects unknown
ASCII-letter prefixes and extra positional text. It retains `ArgumentTokenizer` / `ArgumentMultimap`
for optional fields and repeated tags. Repeated single-value prefixes precede index and field validation;
a lone blank `t/` clears tags. Prefix constants and the other command parsers are omitted for readability.
* Once parsing succeeds, `LogicManager` executes the command on `Model.copyForCommand()`, saves changed
data, then calls `Model.publish()`. A parse, execution or save error leaves the live model and view intact.
Contact updates retain the student's UUID, insertion position and unrelated `StudentFields`, including
unknown nested JSON. Deletion removes the entire target record. These are execution/storage guarantees,
not responsibilities of the parser classes.
* stores the address book data i.e., all `Student` objects (which are contained in a `UniqueStudentList` object).

* stores the `Student` objects selected by the current filter, such as search results, in a separate _filtered_ list. It exposes this list as an unmodifiable `ObservableList<Student>` that the UI can observe and bind to, so the UI updates when the list changes.
* stores a `UserPrefs` object that represents the user’s preferences (currently, just the GUI settings). This is exposed to the outside as a `ReadOnlyUserPrefs` object.
* does not depend on any of the other three components (as the `Model` represents data entities of the domain, they should make sense on their own without depending on other components)

**Note:** The alternative, arguably more object-oriented, design below keeps a unique list of tags in `StudentDirectory`, and each `Student` references tags from that list. This lets `StudentDirectory` maintain one `Tag` object per unique tag instead of each `Student` holding its own `Tag` objects.
* can save both address book data and user preference data in JSON format, and read them back into corresponding objects.
* is implemented by `StorageManager`, which delegates the actual JSON file access to `JsonStudentDirectoryStorage` and `JsonUserPrefsStorage` (one class per data file).
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component (because the `Storage` component's job is to save/retrieve objects that belong to the `Model`)
Student records keep owner-defined optional values in `StudentFields`, a JSON-node envelope keyed by each
`StudentField` codec's stable key. `JsonAdaptedStudent` captures these values through Jackson's any-field mapping,
so adding `payments` does not require a new top-level JSON property and edits preserve fields owned by other features.
`PaymentHistory.FIELD` owns the `payments` key and represents one student's month-to-status map. Older records without
the key remain unset; malformed payment JSON stays in the envelope until a payment command reads it, which avoids
loading the directory as empty and accidentally overwriting the original file.
The `payment INDEX m/YYYY-MM s/pending|completed` command changes one recorded month. The companion
`payments m/YYYY-MM [s/pending|completed]` command lists recorded entries from the full register, omits unrecorded
students, and does not change selection. Both commands use the same typed history codec and storage key.
The payment mutation uses the same transaction boundary as other updates: the command edits a staged model, the
complete student directory is encoded and atomically saved, and only then does `LogicManager` publish the staged
state. A no-change result skips the save; a save error leaves the live model and UI untouched.
Classes used by multiple components are in the `tutorconnect.commons` package.
This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.
`TutorConnectParser` recognizes the case-sensitive command, then `StudentParameters` checks parameter
boundaries, unknown/unexpected input and required/duplicate parameters. It retains raw values so controls
cannot disappear during trimming. `AddCommandParser` validates `Name`, `Phone`, `Address` in that order and
constructs one complete `Student` (the existing aggregate now represents a student). The three-argument
constructor assigns a UUID and leaves all optional data unset. `StudentText` owns normalization; `Phone`
owns the reusable Singapore-number contract. `Student.isSameStudent` compares normalized name ignoring case
plus canonical phone; full content equality remains separate from UUID identity.
`LogicManager` executes on `Model.copyForCommand()`. `AddCommand` checks duplicates and shared phones against
the complete address book, then stages the append, full-list predicate and new selected UUID. The logic saves
changed data before `Model.publish()` updates the observable model. `JsonStudentDirectoryStorage` serializes the
complete state first; `AtomicJsonFile` writes and forces a sibling temporary file and atomically replaces the
destination. There is no unsafe truncate-in-place fallback. An I/O failure reports the standard save error and
does not publish. Read-only or identical-data operations do not save.
The JSON `persons` array retains insertion order. Each record now stores `id`; older valid records missing IDs
receive deterministic migration UUIDs from normalized name and phone, persisted on the next successful save.
Missing/null optional properties load unset. Existing email/tags and owner-defined JSON properties survive
round trips. `StudentField<T>` lets each owner provide a validated type/codec; `StudentFields` is immutable and
defensively copied, and prevents optional keys from overwriting core fields. F01 does not define other owners'
commands, education/rate/slot types or their final serialization schemas.
After successful execution, `MainWindow` selects the model's UUID through `StudentListPanel`, which scrolls to
the new row. `StudentDetailsPanel` displays the complete record and em dashes for unset optional fields. Errors
leave the list and details untouched. The F02/F03 owner remains responsible for final index/list/delete policy;
see [the shared interface and owner handoff contract](F01Integration.md), whose owner acknowledgement is pending.

Guardian, rate, level and subject commands delegate their staged mutation to the package-private
`StudentFieldUpdate` helper. Each command retains its public constructor, messages and owner-supplied codec.
The helper resolves the displayed index, preserves the stored formatting and selection on equivalent input,
and otherwise replaces only the requested optional field. Saving remains exclusively in `LogicManager`.
Unreadable in-memory level/subject values retain the existing repair-as-unset behavior; file loading still
validates stored fields before publication. `ClearCommand` clears its staged selection before publication,
so an already-saved empty register never attempts to select a removed UUID.
`PaymentHistory` is the optional `StudentField` value stored under the `payments` JSON key. Each student record
already carries a stable UUID, so its sorted `YYYY-MM` to `pending|completed` map represents one status per
student and month. An absent month is unrecorded; pending is an explicit value. The typed codec validates the
whole object during JSON load, leaving older records without `payments` unset and rejecting malformed months,
types or statuses safely. Editing preserves the UUID and optional-field envelope; deleting the student removes
`PaymentCommandParser` uses the shared structural parser and `VisibleIndex`. It validates the displayed index
syntax before the month and status, then `PaymentCommand` resolves the row against the currently filtered list.
Setting an identical typed status returns a no-change result without staging a mutation. A new or replacement
status updates only its month, selects the student and leaves all other fields untouched. The existing
`LogicManager` copy-for-command, save-before-publish flow makes storage failure atomic for the saved file, model,

The proposed undo/redo mechanism is facilitated by `VersionedStudentDirectory`. It extends `StudentDirectory` with an undo/redo history, stored internally as a `studentDirectoryStateList` and `currentStatePointer`. Additionally, it implements the following operations:
* `VersionedStudentDirectory#commit()` -- Saves the current address book state in its history.
* `VersionedStudentDirectory#undo()` -- Restores the previous address book state from its history.
* `VersionedStudentDirectory#redo()` -- Restores a previously undone address book state from its history.
These operations are exposed in the `Model` interface as `Model#commitStudentDirectory()`, `Model#undoStudentDirectory()` and `Model#redoStudentDirectory()` respectively.
Given below is an example usage scenario and how the undo/redo mechanism behaves at each step.

Step 1. The user launches the application for the first time. The `VersionedStudentDirectory` will be initialized with the initial address book state, and the `currentStatePointer` pointing to that single address book state.

Step 2. The user executes `delete 5` command to delete the 5th student in the address book. The `delete` command calls `Model#commitStudentDirectory()`, causing the modified state of the address book after the `delete 5` command executes to be saved in the `studentDirectoryStateList`, and the `currentStatePointer` is shifted to the newly inserted address book state.

Step 3. The user executes `add n/David …​` to add a new student. The `add` command also calls `Model#commitStudentDirectory()`, causing another modified address book state to be saved into the `studentDirectoryStateList`.
**Note:** If a command fails its execution, it will not call `Model#commitStudentDirectory()`, so the address book state will not be saved into the `studentDirectoryStateList`.

Step 4. The user now decides that adding the student was a mistake, and decides to undo that action by executing the `undo` command. The `undo` command will call `Model#undoStudentDirectory()`, which will shift the `currentStatePointer` once to the left, pointing it to the previous address book state, and restores the address book to that state.

**Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index 0, pointing to the initial StudentDirectory state, then there are no previous StudentDirectory states to restore. The `undo` command uses `Model#canUndoStudentDirectory()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will return an error to the user rather
than attempting to perform the undo.

Similarly, how an undo operation goes through the `Model` component is shown below:

The `redo` command does the opposite — it calls `Model#redoStudentDirectory()`, which shifts the `currentStatePointer` once to the right, pointing to the previously undone state, and restores the address book to that state.

**Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index `studentDirectoryStateList.size() - 1`, pointing to the latest address book state, then there are no undone StudentDirectory states to restore. The `redo` command uses `Model#canRedoStudentDirectory()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will return an error to the user rather than attempting to perform the redo.

Step 5. The user then decides to execute the command `list`. Commands that do not modify the address book, such as `list`, will usually not call `Model#commitStudentDirectory()`, `Model#undoStudentDirectory()` or `Model#redoStudentDirectory()`. Thus, the `studentDirectoryStateList` remains unchanged.

Step 6. The user executes `clear`, which calls `Model#commitStudentDirectory()`. Since the `currentStatePointer` is not pointing at the end of the `studentDirectoryStateList`, all address book states after the `currentStatePointer` will be purged. Reason: It no longer makes sense to redo the `add n/David …` command. This is the behavior that most modern desktop applications follow.

TutorConnect targets freelance private home tutors who:
* work independently, without administrative staff, and manage multiple students across Primary, Secondary and Junior College levels;
* need to keep student and parent contact details organised alongside lesson schedules, subject syllabi and academic notes;
* regularly look up or update student information when planning lessons or contacting parents;

1. **Platform Independence**: Should work on any mainstream operating system (Windows 10/11, macOS 12+, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS or later) that has Java `17` or higher installed.
2. **Portability**: Should run out-of-the-box as a single, standalone executable `.jar` file without requiring an installer or external configuration tools.

3. **Architecture Constraint**: Must not depend on any remote server, third-party backend API, or cloud infrastructure; all application logic and data processing must execute locally on the user's host machine.
4. **Capacity**: Should be capable of holding up to 1,000 student and parent contact profiles without noticeable degradation in performance.

5. **Responsiveness**: Any command execution (including searches, filters, and batch updates) should return feedback to the user interface within 1.0 second under normal operating conditions on a standard personal computer.
6. **Startup Time**: Should launch to a fully responsive, interactive GUI ready to receive commands within 3.0 seconds of invocation.

7. **CLI Preference**: A user with an above-average typing speed (greater than 60 words per minute) should be able to accomplish everyday contact and scheduling management tasks faster using CLI commands than through GUI navigation (mouse clicks).
8. **Learnability**: A novice tutor who has basic keyboard familiarity should be able to execute core commands (add, list, find, delete) within 15 minutes of referring to the User Guide.

9. **GUI Clarity**: The graphical user interface should display all vital student contact details and tags legibly across standard display resolutions ranging from $1280 \times 720$ to $1920 \times 1080$.

10. **Data Persistence & Format**: User data must be stored locally in an unencrypted, human-editable text file (e.g., JSON). If the file is modified externally and becomes corrupted, the application should fail safely, notify the user, and start with an empty or backup state rather than crash unexpectedly.
11. **Fault Tolerance**: The application should gracefully handle invalid CLI inputs and malformed flags by presenting clear, actionable error messages without crashing or terminating the session.
12. **No Relational DBMS**: Must not depend on a heavyweight external relational database management system (e.g., PostgreSQL, MySQL); local file I/O must suffice for all data persistence.

13. **Data Security**: Because TutorConnect stores sensitive student and parent contact details (e.g., home addresses, mobile numbers, hourly tutoring fees), no tracking telemetry, analytics, or user data should ever be transmitted outside the local machine.

* **Private contact detail**: A contact detail that is not meant to be shared with others

The shared `StudentParameters` parser preserves raw values until validation. A boundary is a token beginning
with ASCII letters followed by `/`. Thus `a/12/3 Street` is one address, while `x/value` is an
unknown parameter. Slashes embedded in tokens (e.g. `Math/Science`) remain data. Prefix-like literal tokens
are reserved syntax and cannot be escaped. Owners should raise any disagreement with this boundary rule.
Unknown parameter/unexpected preamble checks precede required/duplicate parameter checks, then values are
validated in command documentation order. Empty values are invalid values, not missing prefixes.

when data changed, and calls `Model.publish()` only after successful storage. Errors leave the live model,
filter and selected UUID untouched. Read-only/no-change commands must not write storage.
`AtomicJsonFile` writes and forces a sibling temporary file before atomic replacement. Unsupported atomic
moves fail safely; there is no truncate-in-place fallback. JSON keeps the existing `persons` array in order.

* The project uses the `java.util.logging` package for logging.
* A class obtains a `Logger` with `LogsCenter.getLogger(Class)`, which logs messages at the configured level.
* Log messages are written to the console and a `.log` file.
* The output logging level can be controlled by changing the `LOG_LEVEL` constant in the `LogsCenter` class.
* **When choosing a level for a log message**, follow the conventions given in [_[se-edu/guides] Java: Logging conventions_](https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/java/logging.html).
`WARNING` | A save that failed (staged changes discarded, with the cause), a `list` reload that failed, and a temporary save file that could not be deleted
`INFO` | Startup and shutdown, and each command that saved, with the number of students saved

`FINE` | Command receipt, parse/execution rejection, the parsed command type, unchanged commands that skipped saving, completed publication, UI completion/rejection, atomic-write steps, `schedule`/`unschedule` outcomes and the timetable day shown
Command traces identify the command class after parsing succeeds. They do not echo raw input,
arguments, user-facing feedback or validation exception messages. A parse rejection leaves the live
model unchanged; an execution rejection discards the staged copy. The publication message is emitted
only after `Model.publish` succeeds. Routine invalid input uses `FINE`; storage failures use `WARNING`.
This applies to contact commands (`add`, `edit`, `guardian`, `delete`) and other commands using the same pipeline.
Logs can still contain UUIDs, file paths and storage exception causes, and older log files may contain
raw commands. Treat them as personal data. `LogicManagerLoggingTest` covers saves, save failures,
contact command completion, validation rejection and omission of contact values from command traces.

TutorConnect is a **desktop application for freelance tutors to manage student contacts and lesson details**.
It combines typed commands with a graphical student register and details panel.
1. Ensure that Java `25` is installed on your computer (the version used to build and test this release).
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
1. Download the latest `.jar` file from the [team releases](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-F08-3/tp/releases).
1. Copy the file to the folder you want to use as the _home folder_ for TutorConnect.
1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar tutorconnect.jar`.
The application opens with a command box, a feedback area, a student register on the left, and selected-student
details and a weekly schedule on the right. Scroll the details panel to see all fields.

1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
Some example commands you can try:
* `list` : Lists all students and clears selection.
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 a/John street, block 123, #01-01` : Adds a student named `John Doe`.
* `delete 3` : Permanently deletes the 3rd student shown in the current list, without confirmation.

* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add n/NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `edit 1 n/NAME [t/TAG]` can be used as `edit 1 n/John Doe t/friend` or as `edit 1 n/John Doe`.
* Items followed by `...` can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[t/TAG]... ` may be omitted, or written as `t/friend` or `t/friend t/family`.
* Prefixed parameters can be in any order. If a command takes `INDEX`, put it before the prefixed parameters.
For example, if the command specifies `n/NAME p/PHONE_NUMBER`, `p/PHONE_NUMBER n/NAME` is also acceptable.
* Commands and prefixes are lowercase and case-sensitive. Separate tokens with spaces; type one command per line.
An `INDEX` is the current displayed row number, starting at 1, not a stored student ID. After `find`, use the
filtered row numbers. Signs, decimals and leading zeroes such as `01` are not valid indices.
* Extraneous parameters for commands that take no parameters, such as `help`, `exit`, and `clear`, are ignored.

* If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.

the new TutorConnect working directory, creating that folder if needed. Back up any existing destination
file before replacing it, then start the app from that working directory. `preferences.json` is optional;
omitting it uses default window settings and avoids copying off-screen coordinates between computers.
